paragraphs: The Checker is the taxi in every film set in New York before the eighties, and it is recognisable for reasons that have nothing to do with styling: it was built tall and boxy so passengers could get in wearing a hat, with a flat roof, upright glass and enormous rear doors. That deliberate lack of fashion is what makes it read as a taxi rather than as a period sedan.

The mesh is 196,808 polygons and 205,150 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 28 texture maps at a mix of sizes up to 4096x4096. That count is what the chequered livery, the roof light and the door lettering need to sit correctly on a large flat-sided body.

A rigged build sits on this page at $149 for when the wheels turn and the doors open. The static model at $129 covers period film and television, urban visualisation, advertising, games and print. On sale since 2016.

The Xcelsior is the bus most North American cities run, and its shape is set by regulation and by boarding speed: a low floor throughout, a wide front door, a ramp at the kerb and a flat front with a full-width destination sign. The model carries the wheelchair ramp, the roof hatches, the bike rack mounts and the articulated door panels.

The mesh is 211,251 polygons and 221,710 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 15 texture maps - 3 at 4096x4096 and 12 at 2048x2048, which is what a transit livery with route branding requires.

A rigged build sits on this page at $149 for when the wheels turn and the doors open. The static model at $129 covers urban and transit visualisation, city planning presentation, municipal marketing, street scenes and games. On sale since 2016.

A cheetah is the hardest big cat to animate. The spine flexes further than any other feline, the legs are longer relative to the body, and the whole gallop depends on that spinal extension - a rig built for a lion will not produce a cheetah's run. This build arrives rigged and prepared for Maya, with that spine already solved.

That preparation is where the value sits. Rigging a quadruped is slow work, and rigging one whose defining movement is an extreme spinal cycle is slower still. Delivered ready for the application it will be animated in, the animal is usable on day one.

A build prepared for Cinema 4D sits on this page at $149. This one at $119 is built to CheckMate specification and aimed at wildlife documentary, natural history and education material, advertising, film and television, and games. On sale since 2020.

A RoPax ferry carries vehicles and passengers at once, and the hull shows both jobs: a vehicle deck with a stern ramp low in the hull, passenger accommodation stacked above it, and a fine bow because this class is built for speed rather than volume. The model keeps the ramp, the lifeboat davits, the mast array and the funnel casings.

It runs 261,946 polygons and 281,485 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 30 texture maps at a mix of sizes up to 4096x4096. Thirty maps is what an operator livery on a long white hull needs to avoid visible repetition.

Three other builds sit on this page, including a catamaran at $119 and rigged versions at $149 and $99. Aimed at maritime and transport visualisation, ferry operator marketing, port and harbour scenes, and games. On sale since 2019.

The M119 is a light gun designed to be slung under a helicopter and set down where heavier artillery cannot go. Everything about it is built around weight: a tubular carriage, split trails, a small shield and a firing platform that drops under the axle. The model carries the trails, the platform, the sights and the recoil assembly that define the piece.

The mesh runs 215,063 polygons and 223,922 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 20 texture maps - 15 at 4096x4096 and 5 at 2048x2048, carrying the chipped olive paint and the stencilled markings.

A rigged build sits on this page at $149 for when the trails spread or the barrel elevates. The static model at $119 covers defence visualisation, documentary and news graphics, training material, film and television, and games. On sale since 2018.

A ground radar in the deployed state looks nothing like it does on the road. The array is raised and tilted back, the outriggers are down, the generator and control shelter are set out beside it and cabling runs between them. That deployed arrangement is what a defence render usually needs, and it is what this build shows.
The mesh runs 232,413 polygons and 251,113 vertices in quads and tris with mixed UV layout, with the detail concentrated in the array face, the trailer frame and the support equipment.

A rigged build sits on this page at $129 for when the array has to raise or rotate. The static model at $99 covers defence and air defence visualisation, news and documentary graphics, procurement and training presentation, and games. Built to StemCell specification, on sale since 2026.

For twenty years the Crown Victoria was the American police car, and its silhouette is burned into every viewer's memory: a big rear-drive sedan with a long bonnet, a squared roof and a light bar across it. Any contemporary saloon dressed in police livery reads as wrong to an audience that grew up on this shape.

The mesh is 153,347 polygons and 166,853 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 8 texture maps at a mix of sizes up to 4096x4096, which carries the department markings and the reflective striping.

This page is unusually deep: rigged builds at $149, including versions prepared for Cinema 4D and for Maya, a generic police car at $149 and full-interior builds at $129. This simple-interior model at $99 suits urban and law enforcement visualisation, film and television, and games. On sale since 2016.

A near-future combat suit has to look engineered rather than styled: armour plates sized to the body segments that actually need protection, joints left flexible, cabling routed where it would not snag, and a helmet with a real sensor package rather than a smooth visor. This build follows that logic, which is what separates plausible military science fiction from costume design.

The mesh is 125,228 polygons and 128,832 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs. That budget goes into the plate edges and the joint hardware, which is where a suit is examined in close-up.

At $99 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits games, science fiction film and television, previsualisation and concept work, illustration and trailers. On sale since 2025, kept to real-world scale so it fits a standard human figure.

A warship bridge is a working room rather than a set: consoles arranged for sightlines out of the windows, the captain's chair positioned where it can see both, repeaters and telegraphs within reach, and windows raked forward to cut reflection. Those relationships are what make a bridge convincing, and they cannot be improvised from photographs of controls.

The mesh runs 304,161 polygons and 337,689 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the detail in the console faces, the window frames and the overhead fittings that fill a camera's frame in a confined interior.
At $99 it suits naval visualisation, film and television interiors, documentary and museum material, training and simulator projects, and games. On sale since 2020.

A rice combine is built for flooded fields, and that changes the machine completely: it runs on rubber tracks rather than wheels so it does not sink, it is narrow enough for paddy bunds, and the header is set low for a crop that grows in standing water. Anyone who has seen one working will spot a wheeled combine dressed up as a rice harvester immediately.
The mesh is 198,198 polygons and 202,998 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 11 texture maps at 4096x4096, carrying the mud, the paint and the manufacturer markings.

A rigged build sits on this page at the same $99 for when the tracks move or the header runs. Aimed at agricultural machinery marketing, farming visualisation, agritech presentation, rural scenes and games. Built to StemCell specification, on sale since 2020.

A fighter pilot's kit is a system: a flight suit, an anti-g garment over the legs, a torso harness, a survival vest, gloves and a helmet with an oxygen mask. Each layer changes the silhouette, and the bulk sits in specific places - around the thighs, across the chest - which is why a smooth jumpsuit with a helmet never reads correctly.

The mesh is 61,863 polygons and 64,611 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 21 texture maps at 4096x4096. That budget carries the webbing, the buckles, the patches and the fabric weave that make flight gear look used.

A second build sits on this page at the same $99. Both suit military aviation visualisation, film and television costume reference, documentary work, games and training material. On sale since 2017, kept to real-world scale so it fits a standard figure.

A rear suspension assembly is one of the most photographed things in automotive marketing and one of the least understood: control arms, uprights, coilovers, anti-roll bar, driveshafts and brake discs all arranged in a geometry that determines how the car behaves. Showing it correctly is what makes an engineering claim in an advertisement credible.
The mesh is efficient at 39,098 polygons and 41,669 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the density in the joints, the spring coils and the disc detail rather than in bulk.

At $99 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits automotive engineering presentation, technical marketing and cutaways, motorsport and performance advertising, education material and games. On sale since 2024.

A truck chassis is the honest part of a lorry: two steel rails, crossmembers between them, axles, springs, fuel tanks and the air lines and cabling routed along the frame. Bodybuilders and fleet buyers look at exactly this, because it determines what can be mounted on it and where.

The mesh is 170,052 polygons and 175,444 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 7 texture maps at a mix of sizes up to 4096x4096. The textures carry the frame paint, the galvanising and the road dirt that a chassis picks up first.
At $99 it suits commercial vehicle and bodybuilder presentation, fleet and manufacturer marketing, engineering and technical material, workshop scenes and games. On sale since 2018.

An industrial shredder is a violent machine wrapped in a very plain box. The interest is in the working end: the rotor with its hammers or cutters, the feed hopper wide enough to swallow a car door, the discharge conveyor and the heavy drive motor bolted to one side. This build shows it working, which is why the feed and discharge sides both matter.
The mesh runs 279,847 polygons and 297,412 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the density in the rotor, the hopper mouth and the frame bracing.

At $99 and built to StemCell specification, it suits recycling and waste industry visualisation, equipment marketing and catalogues, sustainability and circular economy presentation, industrial interiors and games. On sale since 2024.
